kicker: Ember · Science · Filling the test gaps
title: Food tests, enzymes and alveoli: learn it, then try it
sub: You told us what caught you out in the test. Each part starts with a short Learn it box. Read it first, then try the questions. About 25 minutes on screen, then a short written paper.
skill: The Because Chain: feature → what it does → why that helps.
target: Two kinds of marks were missing: facts (which test, which enzyme, where it comes from) and links (why each alveolus feature helps). Learn the facts from the boxes, then link every feature to what it does.

blocks.html:
Learn it: four tests, four colour changes
Testing forAddNo (start colour)Yes, it is there
Starchiodine solutionorange-brown (yellow-brown)blue-black
Sugar (e.g. glucose)Benedict’s solution, then heat in a hot water bath for a few minutesbluegreen → yellow → brick-red (more sugar = further along)
ProteinBiuret reagent (no heating)bluepurple (lilac)
Lipids (fats and oils)ethanol, shake, then pour into waterstays clearcloudy white (an emulsion)
Your class may also have used Sudan III for lipids: a red layer on top means lipid. Memory hook: Sugar needs Steam (Benedict’s is the only one you heat).

blocks.q: You add iodine solution to some crushed potato. It turns blue-black. What does that tell you?
blocks.why: Iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is there.

blocks.q: Which food test needs heating in a hot water bath?
blocks.why: Only Benedict’s needs heat. Sugar needs steam.

blocks.q: A drink is tested with Benedict’s solution and heated. It goes brick-red. What does this show?
blocks.why: Blue = none. Green, then yellow, then brick-red = more and more sugar.

blocks.q: Biuret reagent is added to egg white. What colour shows protein is there?
blocks.why: Biuret goes from blue to purple (lilac) with protein.

blocks.q: Some butter is shaken with ethanol and poured into water. What shows a lipid is there?
blocks.why: Lipid forms tiny droplets in the water (an emulsion), which look cloudy white.

blocks.stem:
Some types of fungal cell are grown to produce high-protein food.
The high-protein food can be used to make meat-free burgers.
blocks.q: Which chemical could be used to test if the burgers contain protein?

blocks.html:
Learn it: what an enzyme does
  • Big food molecules (starch, protein, lipids) are too big to pass into the blood. Enzymes break them into small molecules that can be absorbed in the small intestine.
  • An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it speeds up a reaction and is not used up. It can be used again and again.
  • Lock and key: each enzyme has an active site with a special shape. Only one substance (the substrate) has the right shape to fit it, like a key in a lock. The substrate binds to the active site, is broken into smaller molecules (the products), and the products are released.
  • That is why each enzyme works on only one kind of food molecule.

blocks.q: Which is true about an enzyme after it has broken down a food molecule?
o: It is unchanged and can be used again
It is absorbed into the blood
blocks.why: A catalyst is not used up. What is “left behind” is the enzyme (unchanged) plus the small product molecules.

blocks.q: Why does amylase break down starch but not protein?
o: Only starch has the right shape to fit amylase’s active site
Amylase only works in the mouth
blocks.why: The substrate and the active site have complementary shapes (lock and key).

blocks.q: Tap the steps in order.
items: Starch fits into the active site of amylase.
It fits because their shapes are complementary (like a key in a lock).
Bonds in the starch are broken, making smaller sugar molecules.
The sugars are released and the amylase is ready to be used again.
blocks.done: Bind, fit, break, release. That is the 3-mark lock and key answer.

blocks.stem: Amylase is an enzyme that breaks down starch.
blocks.q:
Explain how amylase breaks down starch.
Answer in terms of the ‘lock and key theory’.

points.t: starch / substrate binds to the active site (of the enzyme). (“fits” alone is ignored)
(because) the shape of the active site and the substrate are complementary (allow: they fit together)
a chemical reaction makes smaller molecules / bonds in the starch are broken to make smaller molecules (allow maltose / sugars)

sections.h: 3. Which enzyme, where, and what is left
sections.sub: Read the box first. This was the part you weren’t sure of.

blocks.html:
Learn it: the three enzymes (plus bile)
EnzymeMade inBreaks downMakes
Amylase (a carbohydrase)salivary glands, pancreas, small intestinestarchsugars (maltose, then glucose)
Proteasestomach, pancreas, small intestineproteinsamino acids
Lipasepancreas, small intestinelipids (fats and oils)fatty acids and glycerol
Patterns that help: the pancreas and small intestine make all three. Only amylase is made in the mouth (saliva). Only protease works in the stomach (it likes acid).

Bile is not an enzyme. It is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It breaks fat into small droplets (more surface area for lipase) and neutralises stomach acid.

After digestion: the small molecules (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) are absorbed into the blood in the small intestine. Food that cannot be digested (fibre) goes on to the large intestine.

blocks.q: Which enzyme is in saliva?
blocks.why: Salivary glands make amylase, so starch digestion starts in the mouth.

blocks.q: Which enzyme works in the stomach?
blocks.why: The stomach makes protease, which works well in acid.

blocks.q: What are proteins broken down into?
Which is true about bile?
o: It is an enzyme made in the stomach
It is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and breaks fat into droplets
It breaks protein into amino acids
It is made in the salivary glands
blocks.why: Bile is not an enzyme. It helps lipase by giving it more surface area.

blocks.q: Which organ makes amylase, protease and lipase?
blocks.why: The pancreas (and the small intestine) make all three. The liver makes bile, not enzymes.

blocks.q:
Lipases break down lipids.
Which two products are formed when lipids are broken down?

blocks.stem: Amylase is an enzyme that breaks down starch.
blocks.q: Name the three parts of the human digestive system that produce amylase.

points.t: all three of: salivary gland, pancreas, small intestine (“mouth” and “intestine” on their own don’t count; large intestine is wrong)
or only two of them right

mark.note: Give yourself 2 for all three, or 1 for two of them (not both).

sections.sub: Read the box first. In a 6-marker, every feature needs its link.

blocks.html:
Learn it: feature → what it does → why that helps
Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. Each feature makes diffusion faster.
FeatureWhat it doesSo…
Millions of tiny alveolia very large surface areamore oxygen can diffuse at once
Walls are thin (one cell thick), and so are the capillary wallsa short distance for gases to diffuseoxygen gets into the blood faster
A big network of capillaries (good blood supply)blood keeps carrying oxygen away and bringing carbon dioxidekeeps a steep concentration gradient, so diffusion stays fast
Breathing (ventilation)keeps bringing fresh air inoxygen stays high in the alveoli, so the gradient stays steep
Moist lininggases dissolveso they can diffuse across
Careful: say the walls are thin. Not “the alveoli are thin”, and never “thin cell walls” (animal cells have no cell wall).

blocks.q: Why do lungs have millions of tiny alveoli instead of one big bag?
o: To give a much larger surface area, so more oxygen diffuses at once
blocks.why: Lots of small sacs = a huge surface area for diffusion.

blocks.q: Why does a one-cell-thick wall help?
o: It makes a short diffusion distance, so gases diffuse faster

blocks.q: Why does a good blood supply speed up gas exchange?
o: Blood pushes air into the alveoli
Blood keeps taking oxygen away, so there is always less oxygen in the blood than in the alveoli (a steep concentration gradient)
Blood adds oxygen to the alveoli
blocks.why: Moving blood keeps the gradient steep, so oxygen keeps diffusing in.

blocks.q: Tap the links in order for one feature.
items: The alveoli walls are only one cell thick.
So the oxygen has a short distance to diffuse.
So oxygen diffuses into the blood quickly.
So the body gets enough oxygen for respiration.
blocks.done: A 6-marker wants about three features, each with its link like this.

blocks.q:
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli in the lungs.
Describe three features of the alveoli that help maximise gas exchange.

points.t: (large) capillary network / many capillaries / good blood supply
walls are thin / one cell thick (“alveoli are thin” and “thin cell walls” don’t count)

mark.note: In this question “moist” and “steep concentration gradient” score nothing: the marks are for the three features.

blocks.html:
Learn it: three kinds of variable
  • Independent variable: the one you change on purpose.
  • Dependent variable: the one you measure (it depends on what you changed).
  • Control variables: the ones you keep the same so the test is fair.
The spring: you hang masses on it and measure the extension. You change the force (the weight of the masses), so that is the independent variable. The extension is the dependent variable. Using the same spring is a control variable.

Your answer “the mass and the force applied” was really the same thing said twice: the weight of the masses is the force. AQA accepts force, weight or mass. Next time, write just one: “the force on the spring”.

blocks.stem: A student investigated how the force applied to a spring affects the length of the spring.
blocks.q: What is the independent variable in this investigation?
o: The force applied to the spring
blocks.why: Mark scheme: force (applied to spring) or weight (of the masses); allow mass hung from spring.

blocks.q: In the same investigation, what is the dependent variable?
o: The length (or extension) of the spring

blocks.q: A student tests amylase at 10, 30, 60 and 90 °C. Which is the independent variable?
blocks.why: Temperature is what the student changes. The iodine colour is what they observe, and the volume of starch is kept the same (a control).

blocks.html: Print the written paper and do it by hand. Q3 is the 6-marker: write three features, and give every one its link (feature → what it does → why that helps). Mark it with the answers on the last page.

items: I can say all four food tests and their colour changes without looking.
I know Benedict’s is the only one you heat.
For each enzyme I can say where it is made, what it breaks down and what it makes.
I know bile is not an enzyme.
Every alveolus feature I wrote has a “so…” after it.

blocks.q: “Why can’t you absorb a piece of bread straight into your blood?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for: starch is too big a molecule → amylase (from salivary glands, pancreas, small intestine) breaks it into sugars → small enough to be absorbed into the blood in the small intestine. Then ask “and what is left of the amylase?” (unchanged, used again).

marking.html:
• 1. Starch: iodine, blue-black. Sugar: Benedict’s (heated), brick-red (or green/yellow/orange). Protein: Biuret, purple/lilac. Lipid: ethanol, cloudy white (or Sudan III, red layer). 1 mark per row, chemical and colour both needed.
  • 2. Amylase: any two of salivary glands, pancreas, small intestine; starch; sugars (maltose/glucose). Protease: any two of stomach, pancreas, small intestine; protein; amino acids. Lipase: pancreas, small intestine; lipids; fatty acids and glycerol. 1 mark per row.
  • 3. Levels (marked like an AQA 6-marker). Level 3 (5–6): at least three features, each clearly linked to how it speeds up diffusion. Level 2 (3–4): features given, some linked. Level 1 (1–2): features listed with no links. Points: millions of alveoli → large surface area → more diffusion at once; walls one cell thick (and thin capillary walls) → short diffusion distance → faster diffusion; network of capillaries / good blood supply → oxygen carried away → steep concentration gradient kept; ventilation brings fresh air → keeps gradient steep; moist → gases dissolve. Oxygen into the blood, carbon dioxide out.
  • 4. (a) the force on the spring (or weight / mass of the masses) (1). (b) e.g. the same spring; the same starting length measured the same way (1).
